content.thinking:
I need to plan the whole module carefully in one pass without testing, so it has to be type-correct and runtime-safe from the start. I'm designing a tall, slender elven ranger archer in high-fantasy anime style with cel shading, gold trim, flowing cape, long hair, and an ornate bow with quiver and arrows, set in a T-pose for the rest position.

Shifting to an A-pose with arms angled slightly down and outward and legs apart, I'm laying out the full skeleton: hips as root, a three-part spine chain, neck, head, jaw, arm chains with shoulder/elbow/wrist/hand, and finger chains (two joints per finger, five fingers per hand) built through a helper function to keep the code manageable. I'm also adding leg IK chains with toes, a long ponytail hair chain, a cape joint chain, and ear joints, using a mirrored coordinate convention where the model faces +Z and left/right sides are handled by a sign multiplier.

I'm now working out precise world-space measurements for an anime-proportioned figure roughly 1.78-1.82m tall — setting floor, ankle, knee, hip, waist, chest, neck, and head heights, aiming for elongated legs and a head size around 7.7 heads tall, while favoring explicit world coordinates and literals over local joint space to avoid left/right confusion.

Now I'm calculating shoulder and hip widths, then working out the A-pose arm positions — shoulder, elbow, and wrist coordinates with slight forward bends and downward-outward angles — while deciding that hands should rest empty in the resting pose, with any bow or weapon prop placed separately on the floor.

For the bow, I'm reconsidering: a held weapon should actually be gripped in the left hand at the side, vertical and slightly forward, with the limbs extending roughly equal lengths above and below the grip so the lower tip nearly touches the floor, giving a natural standing-archer silhouette rigidly parented to the hand joint.

I'll just pick a reasonable orientation without overanalyzing the exact string direction—placing the grip at hand position with limbs curving slightly backward in Z, tips reaching away from the grip point.

Checking that the hand position aligns with the bow grip, I calculate the grip center from the wrist position and verify the bow's tip positions fall within reasonable bounds without touching the floor. For the right hand, I'll keep it relaxed and slightly open, possibly holding an arrow rather than gripping anything else.

Thinking about small magical accents to add character without overcomplicating things - a glowing gem on the bow, glowing arrowheads in the quiver, subtle runes on the cloak trim, and an emerald brooch, all in a teal-cyan anemo-style glow. The overall palette is forest green cloak, cream tunic, gold trim, silver-blond hair, and tan leather accents.

For the body construction, I'm working out the rigging approach: building a spine chain from the hips root through several catmull-rom control points up to the neck base, then sweeping a tube along that chain with an ellipse radius function to form the torso. Setting up joint names...

With 3 names covering 4 points, that gives 3 span joints with no separate tip, so the last spine segment runs up toward the neck, and I'm parenting the neck chain to that final spine joint. Then I'm defining the head joint itself, parented to the second neck joint, positioned at the top of the neck with a slight forward-upward direction.

Continuing with jaw and head geometry, I'm placing a jaw hinge below the head joint and building the skull as a scaled ellipsoid sphere, with a smaller face wedge to give an anime-style narrow chin shape.

Now I'm figuring out eye placement using a decal on a combined skull-and-face surface, calculating the sphere's surface z-coordinate at the eye's x-offset so the eyes sit flush against the curved face.

Using the hit normal as the default direction should work fine since it points outward naturally, and drawing orientation defaults to world up. For mirroring across the two sides, I'll set the mirror condition based on which side value is positive, representing the left side.

For eye placement, I'm sizing them with a decent width and height, positioning them symmetrically around the center with enough gap between the inner edges so they don't overlap. I'll treat the face as a separate surface from the skull cranium, applying the eye decal onto the combined head surface so the projection wraps correctly onto skull and jaw meshes.

Now for the nose, I'm using a small squashed sphere scaled thin and tall to create a subtle bump near the face center. For the mouth, I'm sweeping a thin curved tube with a dusty pink color along a gentle arc to form lips, positioned slightly proud of the face surface so it reads clearly.

Still working out the normal-offset math...

For the mouth and brows, I could drape a rough catmull-rom path onto the skin surface with a small lift so samples snap to the nearest surface point, then sweep a tube along it. For the ears, I'm thinking long pointed elven shapes extruded from a leaf-like outline, swept back and slightly upward.

Still writing ear outline...

Computing orthogonal thickness direction...

I also need ear joints on the head for a flick motion, with a pink inner-ear strip slightly thicker than the outer ear so it peeks through both faces, plus a small gold torus earring at the lobe.

For hair, I'm sculpting a silver-blond cranium cap as a stretched sphere positioned to cover the top and back of the skull, checking the geometry math to make sure the hairline sits properly against the front of the head without clipping through it.

I'm also planning bangs and side locks as flattened, tapered blade-like shapes swept along curves from the hairline, using a helper function that generates these tube shapes with squashed radii to frame the face naturally.

For the hair color, I'm applying a cel-shaded paint with a vertical gradient from lighter blonde at the top to a darker tone near the tips, so the shading reads with proper depth.

Now I'm working out the ponytail chain, attaching it high at the back of the head and routing a curved path downward with a slight wave, while making sure it sits correctly relative to the cape so the two don't visually collide at the back.

I could build the cape as a membrane stretched between a top edge across the shoulders and a bottom hem edge, skinning it to a spine bone for rigid deformation, or alternatively rig it as a chain of cape joints rooted at the spine with the membrane edges following those chains.

I'll go with bone: capeChain for the membrane, since the doc confirms bones can follow a Chain's nearest point, and default smooth skinning should blend naturally across the width. Now I need to check that the cape doesn't clip through the torso's back, since the surface sits close to the shoulder blade depth at the top edge.

Working out the hem shape...

Actually I'll keep the cape membrane simple and handle the detail through paint instead: a dark green to lighter gradient with a gold trim line near the hem, using cel-shaded coloring based on position across the cape.

Now checking the ponytail positioning against the cape so it doesn't clip -- I'm computing the cape's z-depth at different heights along its curve and comparing against where I want the hair to fall, adjusting the hair's end point so it sits believably behind the cape rather than poking through it.

Checking the ponytail clearance near the neck at y=1.55, I confirm it passes behind safely. I'll skip the hood and instead add a gold-trimmed leaf-shaped mantle over the shoulders, then set up the ponytail's joint chain with four hair segments parented to the head.

For the outfit I'm planning a cream tunic with gold-trimmed hem, green leather bracers, dark-green trousers, brown knee-high boots, a belt pouch, and a baldric holding a back quiver with visible fletchings, plus small leaf-shaped pauldrons with gold edging on both shoulders for that ornate anime look.

I'm also adding a gold circlet with a green gem and a leaf-tiara accent on the forehead, and thinking through how to paint the tunic's gold trim lines procedurally based on position and normal conditions, bumping texture resolution to 2048 for finer detail given the painted surface area.

I'll settle on 2048 for the paint sheet rather than 4096, keeping most body parts as cel-painted surfaces while reserving flat colors for glowing elements like gems, arrowheads, and runes, and checking that texel density stays reasonable across the roughly 9 square meters of painted area.

Since this is a single clean pass with no verification step, I need to write carefully typed code using a limited, safe set of builder functions—joint, chain, sweep, rod, spike, part, extrude, lathe, membrane, stick, surface, decal—and make sure imports stay minimal since unused ones will error, double-checking what types like Joint and Chain the skeleton module actually exports before relying on them.

Now I'm defining the color palette: skin tones, hair gradients with shadow fallbacks, and setting up a `Col` type alias for string-or-Paint values to keep helper signatures consistent.

Defining more color palettes...

I'm working out the limb coverage: cream tunic sleeves to the elbow, green leather bracers with gold trim over the forearms, and bare-fingered hands. For the palette I'm settling on emerald green, cream, gold, brown leather, and cyan glow accents, with tight dark trousers covering the legs.

I'm finalizing colors for contrast: dark forest trousers, brown boots with gold cuffs, cream tunic with an emerald panel, emerald cloak, and platinum-silver hair with violet-blue shadows against warm pink skin and emerald-teal eyes. Now I'm starting to build the skeleton, defining the hip joint as the root of the spine hierarchy.

Now I'm working out the leg chains—placing hip sockets, computing thigh and shin lengths against the ankle target distance to determine knee bend, and naming the joints along each limb.

Still defining joint names...

I'm giving the toe chain a "digit" role and parenting it to the leg's tip joint, then considering the rest pose so boots sit flush on the floor with minimal clearance.

For the leg meshes, I'm sweeping thigh and shin together along the leg chain with tapering radius for trousers, then adding a separate boot sweep over the lower portion with a gold cuff accent, using the chain's from/to cropping to split trouser and boot regions along the same leg geometry.

I'm deciding the boots should reach just below the knee with a fold-down gold cuff, and the trousers get covered where the larger-radius boot overlaps them. Using flat end caps lets the boot top close cleanly while the gold cuff ring sits over the seam.

Now I'm working out the torso as a separate sweep from pelvis to shoulders, adding a distinct hip ellipsoid, and tuning radii at waist, chest, and shoulder points to keep the figure slim and androgynous.

I'll add shoulder-root spheres and a sloped trapezius piece, then plan the tunic as a flared skirt with front/back tabard panels extending to mid-thigh, considering a lathe shape for that part.

Simplifying to a faceted 8-segment lathe skirt from waist to hem with a slight flare, defined as a thin quad-loop outline so it has proper wall thickness, with legs hidden inside since the skirt covers them.

I'm checking that the thigh's outer radius doesn't poke through the skirt geometry at various heights, adjusting the skirt's waist and hem radii and tightening the thigh/hip spacing until the numbers clear enough margin at each y-level.

I'm painting the skirt as a faceted lathe shape in cream with a gold hem band based on height, and considering a tabard with a gold border using layered extrude shapes slightly larger underneath for the outline effect.

I'll cap the part count target around 300–500 and write helper functions to generate details efficiently. For the arms, I'm planning joint chains with shoulder, elbow, and wrist points to define the limb segments.

Working out the elbow and wrist positions by projecting direction vectors along the upper arm and forearm, bending slightly forward in z for a natural elbow angle.

I'm modeling the left fist gripping the bow as a vertical cylinder, with the palm wrapped around it and fingers curling as short capsule arcs around the grip axis at stacked height offsets.

Mapping out finger placement as arcs curling around the grip, with each finger approximated by a small curve of points around the vertical cylinder radius.

This is getting too fiddly to nail precisely in one blind pass. I'll simplify: skip detailed finger-wrap geometry and instead rig the hand as a palm sphere with four finger capsule chains, letting a simpler rest-pose spec handle the grip illusion.

Rather than forcing a closed fist grasping the bow, maybe the cleanest rigging-friendly solution is slinging the longbow across the back with the quiver, so both hands stay open and relaxed in a neutral readable pose — though I worry the diagonal strap might clash visually with the cape and ponytail.

Settling on the bow held vertically in the left hand with digit chains wrapping the grip, and building a reusable finger helper to generate joint chains for both hands—curled fingers gripping the bow on the left, spread and extended fingers on the open right hand.

Working out the right hand's wrist position, direction vector, and palm/finger/thumb lengths to position the relaxed open hand in space.

Confirming the lateral axis points front-back for finger spread, consistent for both hands with thumb forward on the +lat side. Now I'm defining a generic finger-building function that computes joint points from the base, direction, lateral offset, segment lengths, and curl angle.

Working out the curl: I'm rotating the finger direction toward the palm normal (inward toward the body) by an accumulating angle, using a sign flip between left and right hands so the normal points correctly, then orthogonalizing against the finger direction before applying the rotation. For the thumb, I'm positioning its base near the wrist on the palm side and angling its direction toward the lateral axis.

Now I'm laying out the finger segment lengths — index, middle, ring, pinky each with three segments of decreasing size — and working through a consistent left-hand geometry, computing the palm center and knuckle line position from the wrist point and hand direction vector so the fingers attach correctly around the grip.

Thinking about the bow grip itself, I realize holding a vertical rod means the forearm must be oriented so the rod runs roughly parallel to it, like gripping a cane or hammer handle, with the thumb resting on top and the fingers curling around the shaft.

I'm comparing grip angles for different handle orientations—a hammer's power grip sits the handle oblique to the forearm by roughly 45-60°, while gripping a vertical cane with a hanging arm aligns the handle axis with the forearm, with slight ulnar deviation at the wrist.

Working out the fist geometry, placing the wrist above and behind the grip center, then curling fingers around the palm with a defined radius and positioning the thumb wrapping the opposite side.

Calculating left-hand finger positions...

Let me reconsider the wrap angle: finger length relative to palm radius gives arc angle ≈0.075/0.027≈2.8 rad, roughly 160°, so each finger segment needs to sweep about that much around the curl rather than the full 280° I tried.

I'll simplify by just picking fingers to start at the back-inner knuckle position and let the palm/thumb occupy the opposite half, without overanalyzing the exact geometry further.

I'm sizing the palm ellipsoid to sit near the grip, then working out the leather-wrapped handle dimensions and finger radius/spacing so the fist covers the grip without visible gaps.

Now I'm plotting finger joint curves using angle lists for each finger (pinky shorter than the rest), checking that segment arc lengths sum correctly, then positioning the thumb wrapping over the index finger near the top of the grip.

Setting up the arm sweep with shoulder-to-wrist radius tapering and sleeve/skin color bands, then layering the gold bracer sweep over the forearm segment...

I'm also planning cuff rings as shorter radius-bumped sweeps, confirming the chain naming convention gives a tip joint at the hand, and considering a shoulder sphere plus pauldron shape to seal the joint gap.

For the pauldron I'm layering a lathed emerald dome, a gold rim torus, a gold leaf accent, and a gem stud on top for detail, then moving on to torso tunic paint with a center line.

Now I'm defining a paint function for the tunic that uses world coordinates to draw a gold V-neckline trim, center gold buttons, and lace details in green, then adding a baldric strap that drapes diagonally across the chest as a swept leather tube.

I'm figuring out the cross-section shape for the strap—trying a box section versus an elliptical sweep, since the orientation of the sweep's normal is ambiguous and could make the strap render edge-on if I get the frame wrong.

Setting up the path with `up: [0,0,1]` so the normal stays pointed outward across the chest as the diagonal strap wraps from shoulder to hip, relying on parallel transport to keep it consistent over the shoulder curve.

Twisting around a closed loop seems risky, so I'll skip the box-section strap idea and just go with a simple round cord geometry instead, adding gold studs to make it read as a cord baldric.

For the belt, I think a lathe-generated ring is actually cleaner than a swept circle—rotating a flat band profile around the vertical axis avoids the orientation/roll problems entirely and gives a proper flat belt shape, with a separate buckle piece added on.

I should give the torso sweep 12 sides for smoother geometry, matching the belt's 12-segment cylinder, and add a small radius margin so the belt sits just outside the torso surface without clipping. But I still need to account for how the torso radius profile changes along its height near the belt position.

For that, I'm approximating the mapping between y-position and the parametric t-value along the spine path using a simple linear formula, which should be accurate enough given the margin I've built in. I'm deciding to skip fancy hit-based decoration logic for the torso and just use explicit world coordinates and bone assignments instead, passing the bone directly rather than relying on nearest-joint lookup.

Now I'm defining helper functions for adding body parts with geometry, color, bone, and position, then working through the head's construction piece by piece: the skull as an ellipsoid, the lower face, the jaw, and the chin, carefully positioning each so the silhouette reads as an anime-style pointed chin with no visible gaps between the face and jaw pieces.

For facial features, I'm setting up a nose/mouth/eye placement system that finds the nearest hit point on the combined surface of the skull, face, and jaw parts, using the normal at that hit point to orient decals so they face outward correctly from the curved head surface.

Decals inherit the skin weights of whatever they land on, so rigid head parts bind to the head bone fine. I'll leave brows in the base texture since bangs partly cover them anyway, and keep the default blush positioned at the lower outer corner of the eye texture.

Now checking hair cap geometry: comparing its sphere scale and center against the skull dimensions to confirm coverage at the top, sides, and nape, then tracing the front edge of the cap at a few y-heights to see whether it dips below the face surface and stays hidden rather than poking through.

I'm placing the hairline around y~1.755 and planning seven bangs locks sweeping down from there with a center part, plus longer face-framing locks extending down near the chin at the sides, while checking the skull's front radius to make sure they sit flush against the surface.

Checking the face ellipsoid's radius shows the temple-to-cheek face-framing locks actually fall outside the head surface near the cheek, so I'm repositioning them to hang beside the cheeks down to collar level instead. Writing lock sweep helper...

Realizing I had it backwards for the side locks—since the surface normal there points along x, the lock needs to be wide in that axis instead, so I'll swap the radius parameters with a flip flag. Still sketching the ponytail sweep geometry attached to the hair chain...

Adding a small torus ring for the hair tie, placed on the head bone, then working out a gold circlet band that wraps around the forehead as a closed sweep path following the head's cross-section at that height.

I'm adding a gold circlet band with a green front gem and small leaf fins, then working out how the ears attach beneath the hair cap, angling them outward and slightly up so they poke through the sides naturally.

Now I'm designing the torso's collar details — a mantle with a gold leaf-shaped brooch and glowing gem at the throat, positioning it against the chest curve, and sketching out the torso profile radii at each height segment from waist to shoulders.

I'm adding a flattened ellipsoid yoke across the shoulders for width, a shoulder sphere where arms attach, and a slender neck sweep with a gold collar ring to keep the elf's proportions delicate.

For the chest, I'm sweeping a thin gold chain between the mantle clasps with slight sag, sized to sit just outside the torso surface, with small discs capping the ends. Now I'm planning the lower body pieces—trousers, a skirt lathe, belt, pouches—and working out where to tilt a quiver on the back.

I'm realizing the quiver and the ponytail both want to sit at the same back-center depth, so I need to resolve that overlap—maybe move the ponytail to a shoulder or shift the quiver to a hip position, weighing which placement reads better for an elven ranger silhouette.

I'm reconsidering the quiver placement instead — moving it to a hip position angled back with fletchings peeking up near the waist, tilted rakishly backward about 20 degrees so it stays uncluttered. Still torn between that and a classic back quiver, which might mean shortening the ponytail to an upswept style rather than letting it flow long.

Settling on a hip quiver slung at the right-back with a strap, keeping the long ponytail, and adding a small hunting knife and pouch on the left hip for detail. I'm working out the quiver's exact geometry — its tilt axis running from a lower point near the hip bone up and slightly back, checking that its radius clears the thigh and doesn't collide with the skirt's flare at higher y-values.

Defining quiver lathe profile...

Still working out fletching card placement...

Fletching cards use a feather texture in green-cream tones with alpha testing for cutout edges; arrow tips stay hidden in the quiver, showing only nocks and fletching. The right hand stays empty, and I'm designing the bow itself as an elegant recurved elven weapon with leaf-shaped limb tips, gold inlay, and glowing cyan runes, positioning its grip and defining the limb curve mathematically in the Y-Z plane from the grip point upward.

Working out the recurve shape now -- plotting the curve points so the limbs bend toward the string at the midsection before curling forward again at the tips, keeping the total bow height around 1.49 units so it sits proportionally below the elf's head.

I'm also double-checking for collisions: comparing the bow's x-position against the hip/skirt edge and the arm's position at various heights, calculating the gaps between the bow limb and the elbow/arm radius to confirm there's enough clearance (around 0.026 units) without clipping, especially as the upper limb approaches the shoulder height.

I'm planning to construct the bow as a single tapered tube sweeping from lower tip through the grip to the upper tip, using a smooth curve through about nine points with a radius that narrows symmetrically from grip to tips, giving it an oval cross-section wider along the side axis than in depth, then adding gold ornament rings and a painted wood-grain finish.

For coloring, I'm thinking of banding the limb by distance from the grip: gold at the very tips, a thin gold ring transition, and a deep teal lacquer body in between, set against a pale cream-white wood tone so the bow stands distinct from the green outfit, with gold and teal inlay accents near where it rests against the leg.

Now I'm working out the bowstring geometry, running it as a near-straight line between the two tip positions at a slightly offset depth so it passes behind the grip and clears the fist without visually colliding with the palm.

Writing bow decoration details...

All bow parts attach to the left hand bone, with fingers simply resting on the fist. For the belt and pouches, I'm calculating the torso radius at belt height to size an open cylinder for the belt geometry.

Now I'm checking proportions: the skirt's waist radius (0.145) is wider than the belt (0.105), which creates a gap at the waist — realistically the tunic skirt should hug the belt line before flaring out over the hips, so I need to adjust the skirt's top radius to match the waist more closely before it flares outward over the legs.

I need to check the pelvis ellipsoid stays hidden within the hips, then verify the thigh doesn't poke through the skirt interior at the hip socket region, comparing radial distances to confirm clearance.

Now I'm working out the front tabard panel that hangs over the skirt, figuring out how to position its outline so it sits flush against the skirt's front surface.

I need to tilt the panel to follow the skirt's conical slope rather than hanging straight down, since the skirt's radius grows as y decreases. I'm calculating the slope rate and deriving the tilted direction vector so the panel's z-offset shifts appropriately as it moves up or down along y.

Now I'm working out a pointed leaf-shaped outline for the panel in local coordinates, then checking how its width compares to the underlying skirt surface curvature at that radius to make sure the panel edges don't poke through or gap away from the skirt surface.

I decide to layer a bordered emblem into the panel: a larger gold border shape and a smaller inset emerald shape, each with slightly different extrusion thickness so the emerald sits proud of the gold. I mirror the same setup for a back panel using the opposite-facing normal, and work out the outward normal direction via a cross product to confirm the panel faces correctly away from the body.

Now I'm planning the skirt hem trim, a hip pouch and dagger sheath attached at the belt, and a cape built as a flat double-sided membrane with gold trim and a subtle leaf motif at the hem. I think about giving the cape some visual interest by making its hem wavy rather than a straight edge, using alternating offsets along a smooth curve to suggest natural folds.

Still working out cape attachment points...

Maybe I should add the cape as a separate short mantle instead — a flared lathe collar around the neck base that transitions from radius 0.07 to 0.14, dropping from y 1.52 to 1.44, trimmed in gold with emerald accents. That collar would help cover the gap where the cape's top edge sits behind the yoke.

I'm checking that the mantle's radius profile clears the torso surface at each height without poking through, and adjusting the top opening radius to about 0.055 so the neck shows through with a slight open-collar gap rather than clipping.

The mantle's circular cross-section is wider than the torso's flattened depth, so there's a hollow gap visible under the cape at front and back that could look like a floating bowl shape. I'm considering flattening the lathe profile with a non-uniform scale on the depth axis, but lathe geometry doesn't support that directly, so I need another approach to squash it front-to-back.

I'm checking whether the lathe's face winding stays consistent around the closed profile—whether traveling down the outer wall and back up the inner wall preserves correct orientation so the geometry renders properly without culling issues.

Rather than risk inside-out geometry, I'm leaning toward sticking with b.lathe and handling non-circular shapes through post-hoc scaling, though I need to think through how scaling the mesh affects its transform relative to its origin point.

The key issue is figuring out whether scaling the lathe's local axes maps cleanly onto world axes given its orientation, and whether scale transforms apply to meshes directly or get baked into world space differently than bone transforms do.

Given that risk, I'm leaning toward a simpler geometric approach for the shoulder drape instead: skip the mesh-scale complexity and build the mantle from a chunky rolled collar ring around the shoulders using a closed elliptical sweep, paired with extruded petal-like mantle feathers for a more sculpted, draped look.

Writing petal placement math...

So Y should be derived as N×L to guarantee orthogonality, projecting out any component of N along L first. The handedness doesn't matter since the petal shape is symmetric. Now I'm defining the petal outline points in the (L,Y) plane as a pointed leaf shape, and setting up two rings of twelve petals each at different sizes.

For the mantle, I'm layering leaf shapes on the shoulders attaching to the spine bone, with emerald petals inset inside slightly larger gold-bordered petals to create a bordered look, roughly doubling part count to 48. I'm estimating triangle counts per petal after smoothing and figuring the total stays manageable, then working out the ring parametrization around the neck base where each petal root sits, with the inner and outer rings at slightly different radii and heights so they fan outward along the shoulder surface.

Now I'm modeling the shoulder yoke as an ellipsoid and computing surface points at two different latitude angles to place the petal layers near the neck versus farther down, then deriving the normal and downward tangent direction along the ellipsoid meridian so the petals can lie flush against the curved surface -- though I realize the flat petals will poke through the curvature once they extend far enough from their root point.

Rather than fully lathing the mantle edge, I'll just handle it in code and check that the second petal layer, which hangs down toward the back of the yoke, doesn't visually collide with the cape's top edge -- shifting the cape's z-position slightly back and lower should keep the petals rendering in front of it without z-fighting. Next I want to figure out the tunic's back-torso depth.

For the legs, I'm sketching out knee-high boots and a simple two-bone chain from hip to knee to ankle, computing approximate joint positions and forward offsets to approximate a natural bend rather than solving full inverse kinematics.

Now I'm shaping the foot geometry: ankle positioned at y 0.085 with a sole thickness of 0.02 resting at y=0, extending from heel around z -0.065 to toe tip at z +0.20, planning to build it as a swept profile from ankle through ball to toe.

I'm figuring out the radius profile along that sweep so the boot's underside sits flush at the floor, adding a separate thin sole box and tapering the tube's vertical half-height from ankle to ball to toe.

Sole gets dark brown with a small gold toe cap. I'm double-checking the ankle joint placement matches the foot bone in the chain, then moving to the legs—trousers covering the thigh with a smooth tube for the knee bend, and the boot sweep continuing from the midpoint down.

Working out where the boot cuff sits relative to the knee, landing on roughly mid-calf to knee height, with the boot radius tapering down toward the ankle as I define the sweep.

Now I'm mapping the trouser thigh profile and gold cuff rings at the boot tops, then moving on to the sleeve and bracer details before checking off the hands and arms. I'm tracking my remaining component list: torso done, now queuing up neck, head, hair, ears, circlet, bow, quiver, cape, mantle, belt, pouch, and dagger.

I'm skipping pauldrons since the petal mantle covers that area, and deciding on anime flourishes like flowing ribbon tails from the hair tie, a tasseled sash at the hip, and a gold tassel hanging from the bow's grip cord. I want a handful of glowing gem accents — cyan and green flat colors for the circlet, brooch, bow tips, belt buckle, and rune markings — while keeping the overall flat color palette under 64 shades, and I'm still deciding whether to add knee pads to the lower body.

Now I'm checking that every part fits within the model's bounding box — bow width, cape spread, ear reach, total height around 1.82m — and confirming the lowest points like feet, bow tip, and cape hem all sit above the floor plane with a slight sink allowance for the soles. Then I move into defining the exact paint materials, starting with skin tones and a gradient-based hair color with a soft shadow tint.

Defining more material colors...

Still writing V-neck geometry...

Still defining vest color regions...

I'll add small gold eyelet spheres down the center for lacing detail, since the back is hidden under the cape anyway. For the sleeves, I'll paint them cream with gold trim, deciding color based on arm position using a banded fill function.

For the skirt, I'll set up a paint function where the lower portion shifts between gold, emerald, and tunic cream to create a layered banded hem effect, and I'm considering adding small gold leaf-shaped dags hanging around the hem for an extra anime-style flourish.

For the cape, I'm defining its paint based on surface coordinates running from the top edge to the hem, with gold at the very bottom border, a darker emerald band just above it, and the main emerald body filling the rest -- while also thinking through how the inner lining should be colored differently using the face normal, since the cape's outer face points backward.

Now I'm considering the inner lining: when the normal faces inward I'll switch to a cream-teal lining color, and I'm weighing whether to add subtle vertical fold shading or embroidered leaf/vine details using a decal placed on the cape's back surface.

I'm uncertain what type the membrane function returns, so I need to check whether it produces meshes or Parts before I can pass it correctly into a surface or decal call. Applying the decal to the whole root model could be too costly and risk hitting unrelated parts, so I'm thinking about targeting just the cape joint instead, possibly using a type-bypass cast if needed, and considering peeking at the membrane source file to confirm its return type.

Since I have to write the entire module blind in a single reply without reading any files, I'm deciding to skip the decal approach on the cape entirely and instead use a procedural paint pattern — designing a periodic gold diamond-dot lattice based on fractional lattice coordinates to create a repeating motif safely without needing to verify unknown types.

I'm also sketching out how to build the face surface from multiple parts (skull, face, jaw) for decal targeting, and working through the geometry of placing eye decals by finding the nearest point on that surface to a target coordinate in front of the face.

Bangs cover forehead above eyes, so that's fine. For the mouth I'll drape a path along the face skin using the curve points with a slight lift, then sweep that path with a small radius to build the mouth geometry, using a flat mauve color.

Now I'm working out the jaw and head joint structure, placing a jaw joint parented to the head at the jawline, then building the neck chain with two intermediate joints leading up to the head joint near the skull base, and setting the neck sweep radii to taper slightly as it rises.

For facial extras, I'm keeping eyes static, adding eyelashes via texture, small ear piercings, and skipping visible teeth since the mouth stays closed.
